events.title: iMac G3 released
events.summary: Apple began selling the iMac G3 on August 15, 1998 — an all-in-one Mac with USB, no floppy drive, and translucent "Bondi Blue" design.
events.about: The iMac made USB mainstream and gave web designers and developers a stylish Unix-based desktop with Mac OS 8. It sold millions, reviving Apple before the iPod and iPhone. The all-in-one form factor and emphasis on internet out-of-the-box aligned with the late-1990s web boom.

narrative.whyChosen: The iMac G3 saved Apple commercially and pushed USB as the standard peripheral connector.
narrative.whyImportant: It brought millions of new users — and developers — back to the Mac platform.
narrative.problemSolved: Consumers wanted a simple, internet-ready computer without legacy ports and beige boxes.

events.title: Bugzilla 1.0 released
events.summary: Mozilla.org released Bugzilla 1.0 on August 26, 1998 — an open-source bug-tracking system that became the template for web-based issue trackers.
events.about: Bugzilla powered Mozilla, Apache, and thousands of open-source projects before Jira dominated enterprises. Its severity levels, dependency graphs, and email notifications defined how developers filed and triaged bugs online — the ancestor of every modern issue tracker UI.

narrative.whyChosen: Bugzilla was the open-source bug tracker every OSS project used before GitHub Issues.
narrative.whyImportant: It established web-based bug workflows that Jira and others later commercialized.
narrative.problemSolved: Projects tracked bugs in mailing lists and text files with no shared searchable database.
